Palo Alto Soars 7%, Okta Up 11% as DHS Chief Warns of "A Severe Cyber Threat" ©Markus Spiske from Pexels and Yuganov Konstantin via Canva
Key Takeaways

Palo Alto Networks jumped 7% today as Okta, Zscaler, Cloudflare and other cybersecurity stocks rallied on a warning from the Homeland Security secretary of "a severe cyber threat."

The same official said he's "98% confident" recent outages weren't foreign attacks, so investors bought the warning before any new demand showed up.

Palo Alto reports tonight, and the number to watch is Next-Generation Security ARR against a $9.54 billion to $9.56 billion guide.

Palo Alto Networks (PANW:NASDAQ) jumped 7% today, hours before its fiscal first-quarter report, and Okta (OKTA:NASDAQ) rose 11%. Zscaler (ZS:NASDAQ) and Cloudflare (NET:NYSE) each gained 7%.

In prepared testimony for the House Homeland Security Committee, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin warned that adversaries' hackers "retain the capabilities to pose a severe cyber threat to U.S. critical infrastructure." His warning came after a string of outages, from last Friday's nationwide flight ground stop to Microsoft Outlook.

But at the hearing, Mullin said he's "98% confident" the outages aren't malicious activity from foreign adversaries.

The bar just went up

Palo Alto guides to fiscal first-quarter revenue of $3.300 billion to $3.310 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $0.96 to $0.98. Analysts see normalized EPS rising 9% this fiscal year, to $4.18, and another 17% in fiscal 2028:

Palo Alto Networks (PANW): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2028 (years to July) (TIKR)

Palo Alto has beaten estimates seven straight times, yet its stock has fallen 5% on average on report days. And after a slide from its October high, it traded at 74x forward earnings at the last close, above its five-year average of 57x:

Palo Alto Networks (PANW): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)
A read on the whole group

For Okta, the line to watch is Idira, Palo Alto's identity business built on CyberArk, which Palo Alto plans to break out starting this quarter. Idira's pro forma revenue grew 21% in fiscal 2026, nearly twice Okta's 11% growth in its quarter to July 31.

In SASE, Zscaler's home turf, Palo Alto's bookings rose 40% in fiscal 2026. Zscaler reports Dec. 2, a day after CrowdStrike (CRWD:NASDAQ), up 9%, which an Evercore ISI survey named alongside Palo Alto as a leading winner from AI-driven security spending.

Cloudflare's third-quarter revenue grew 39%, and CEO Matthew Prince said "as digital threats escalate, organizations of every size continue to rely on Cloudflare for protection."

Datadog Fell 12% on a Flat Fourth-Quarter Outlook. Analysts Raised Its 2027 Earnings Estimate 6% ©@iJeab via Canva, @kasto via Canva
Key Takeaways

Datadog fell more than 12% on Nov. 4 on a flat fourth-quarter guide, as its largest customer, an AI company, cuts its usage to its contract minimum.

Analysts still raised their 2027 normalized EPS estimate to $3.16 from $2.98, so the whole fall came from a lower multiple.

Cloudflare's higher fourth-quarter guide points to a problem limited to Datadog, and Snowflake reports next, on Dec. 2.

The rising 2027 estimate outweighs the flat quarter, though February's 2027 outlook could pull estimates back down.

Datadog (DDOG:NASDAQ) fell more than 12% on Nov. 4, the day it guided fourth-quarter revenue to $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion. That's flat with the $1.20 billion it had just reported for the third quarter.

But analysts came out of the same report expecting Datadog to earn more in 2027.

On a Nov. 17 episode of the RiskReversal Pod, RBC Capital Markets software analyst Matthew Hedberg put Datadog in a small group: "I have seen clear AI leadership from five or six names that I cover where there's real acceleration like a Datadog or a Cloudflare or CrowdStrike or a Palo Alto and a Snowflake." So Cloudflare (NET:NYSE) and Snowflake (SNOW:NYSE) holders need to know whether one AI customer's cutback stops at Datadog.

One customer, one flat quarter

Third-quarter revenue rose 35%. The trouble is Datadog's largest customer, an unnamed AI company, which is cutting its usage. The fourth-quarter guide counts it only at its minimum commitment, for growth of 25% to 26%, or the low to mid-30s percent without that customer.

Anything it spends above that floor is revenue the guide doesn't count, and CFO David Obstler said it still spent above its minimum in the third quarter. Outside AI, growth is in the high 20s, the fifth straight quarter it has sped up.

As of mid-November, ARKK is down about 4% in 2026, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up about 10%. Her trades keep drawing attention too, including her Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) buying in August. Check out the full story here.

A closer look at ARK's portfolio tells a different story. Many stocks in her portfolio have performed exceptionally well this year. Before we get to them, it helps to know what Wood thinks is driving the market. In an October episode of ARK's "In The Know" series, she spent a good part of the show on AI data centers.

Wood said 90% of all data center financing in the world is in the United States, citing a Bloomberg statistic based on fixed income data. She links that to US tax policy. She expects the money coming into the US to keep pushing the dollar higher.

She also pointed out a risk. The big cloud companies sat on piles of cash for years and never needed to borrow, but they are now selling debt. The price of insuring their debt through credit default swaps has been rising, and she said the neocloud providers are a big part of the reason.

Cathie Wood, Ken Fisher and 10 Other Big Funds Bought Cloudflare, While 9 Sold. Who's Right? ©@da-kuk from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Twelve big funds, including Cathie Wood's ARK Invest and Ken Fisher's Fisher Investments, bought Cloudflare in the quarter ended Sept. 30, while nine sold it.

Cloudflare has fallen 15% since Sept. 30, so the sellers are ahead so far.

Cloudflare's revenue grew 39% in the third quarter, and analysts expect its normalized EPS to double from fiscal 2025 to fiscal 2027.

At about 167x forward earnings, a little below its average since mid-2023, the stock gives the buyers the better case from here, and falling gross margins are the main risk.

Twelve big funds bought Cloudflare (NET:NYSE) in the third quarter, and nine sold it, according to their 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30.

Those counts come from the 456 big funds that had filed for the quarter by Nov. 16. That means funds readers know, or funds with $1 billion or more of US stocks in their 13Fs, leaving out quant and index funds. A buy is a new position or 20% more shares, and a sale is a full exit or a cut of 20% or more. In all, 29 of those funds held Cloudflare on Sept. 30.

Cathie Wood more than tripled her stake

Cathie Wood's ARK Invest, which manages $17.4 billion, took its Cloudflare stake from 175,723 shares to 563,167 in the quarter, a 220% increase. That added about $135 million of stock at quarter-end prices and made Cloudflare 1.1% of ARK's 13F stocks.

The biggest buy came from a fund few investors know. Amanah Holdings Trust, whose 13F holds $1.8 billion of US stocks, opened a new position of 405,992 shares, worth about $141 million. Cloudflare became 7.9% of its 13F stocks and its seventh-biggest holding, which is a real bet for a fund with 21 positions.

Ken Fisher's Fisher Investments, which manages $386.7 billion, added 700 shares, a 57% increase to 1,923. At about $243,000, that's a rounding error for Fisher. Cloudflare ranks 757th among its 1,054 positions.

title: Cloudflare Stock At 38x Sales Faces A Margin Slide
detail:
Cloudflare Stock At 38x Sales Faces A Margin Slide
Trefis Team
Tue, November 17, 2026 at 7:13 AM MST 3 min read
NET
NVDA
^GSPC
AKAM

Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Today's big story: Could Nvidia Stock Fall 50%? Follow The Cash

Cloudflare (NET) stock trades at 38.4 times its sales, against 3.2 times for the S&P 500. Buyers paying that price appear to assume revenue keeps growing near its fiscal Q3 2026 pace of 39.2% and turns into profit. For that to happen, the new business has to earn close to what the old business does on each dollar of sales. So which part of Cloudflare's growth could fall short of that?

Cloudflare's Workers Platform Earns Thinner Gross Margins

During the fiscal Q3 2026 call on November 5, 2026, management said its Workers Developer Platform earns slightly lower gross margins than products such as Zero Trust, though it is far cheaper to sell. That matters because management also named Workers as a main source of the quarter's revenue growth.

Cloudflare's gross margin is falling. It was 71.9% over the twelve months to September 30, 2026, against 75.2% a year earlier. A year before that it was 77.5%, so the margin has fallen in each of the last two years. All three figures are as reported in company filings, not management's adjusted figures. Management's own measure of gross margin, 72.4% in fiscal Q3 2026, is still inside the 70% to 77% range it targets over the long term.

How Much Of Cloudflare Is Exposed To Workers?

Management said on the call that Workers is a big component of almost every pool of funds deal Cloudflare sells, though it does not disclose what percentage of deals include Workers. Pool of funds deals are commitments customers draw down over time. Those deals are part of a business that had $2.73 billion of revenue over the same twelve months, up 35.7% from a year earlier.

Management's case that Workers is cheaper to sell fits the twelve-month figures so far. Cloudflare lost 8.2% of its revenue at the operating line over those twelve months, a smaller loss than the 9.6% a year earlier.

The stock closed on November 16, 2026, 18.7% below its October 9 high, yet its multiple of sales is still far above its low points. At the 29 quarter ends since fiscal Q3 2019, Cloudflare traded as high as 64.2 times sales. At the end of September 2023, it traded at 17.5 times.

How Worried Should Cloudflare Holders Be?

Worried enough to keep an eye on it, not alarmed. The gross margin has given up a few points a year rather than all at once, yet the price appears to assume the slide stops.

Management's own operating margin measure does not show the slide. Management reported an operating margin of 17.5% for fiscal Q3 2026 on its own adjusted measure. On the reported basis, Cloudflare lost 7.3% of its revenue at the operating line in that quarter, a wider loss than the 6.7% a year earlier. Management expects Cloudflare to turn a profit on a GAAP basis in fiscal Q4 2026, which is a forecast, not a result.

Today's big story: Could Nvidia Stock Fall 50%? Follow The Cash

After a rough autumn, several large software stocks look cheap on a popular measure: free-cash-flow yield, the cash a business produced over the past year divided by its stock market value. ServiceNow, trading 42.7% under its peak of the past year, shows a yield of 4.6% at Monday's close. Salesforce shows 8.6%.

Mostly, they are not as cheap as that number says. The yield counts the cash, but not the shares these companies hand employees as pay, and that pay is a real cost to owners: every new share takes a slice of future cash. Subtract stock-based pay and ServiceNow's yield falls to 2.4%. Atlassian's drops from 4.4% to 0.15%, because its stock pay equalled 96.7% of its free cash flow over the past four quarters. Cloudflare and Snowflake turn negative, at -0.23% and -0.45%.

Of the seven names we checked, only Salesforce still yields more than the 10-year Treasury after the adjustment: 6.5% against the 5.1% the Treasury paid on Monday. ServiceNow's headline yield was already below that Treasury rate before stock pay was counted.

The Cost The Headline Yield Leaves Out

Our free cash flow here is operating cash flow minus capital spending, as reported by Morningstar, summed over the last four quarters. For Salesforce, CrowdStrike and Snowflake those four quarters end July 31, 2026; for the others they end Sept 30, 2026. Stock pay is the figure each company adds back in its cash flow statement.

That add-back is the whole issue. Operating cash flow adds stock pay back because no cash leaves the company when it issues shares to staff. But owners still pay, in one of two ways: their stake gets diluted, or the company spends cash buying shares back to stop that from happening. Either way, the headline yield overstates the cash left for people who own the stock.

Jim Cramer and Cathie Wood are two of the most closely followed voices on Wall Street, and we regularly cover the stocks they like. Once a Wall Street darling, Cathie Wood has struggled to replicate her success from the pandemic days as shifting market dynamics have weighed on her disruptive innovation bets. You can see her latest 13F filing here.

Wood's flagship ARK Innovation ETF (BATS:ARKK) is down about 4% so far this year, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up about 10%. ARKK had gained about 16% through the end of September, and a sharp tech selloff in October and early November erased that gain and pushed the fund below where it started the year.  As of Nov. 12, her Ark Innovation ETF has delivered a five-year annualized return of -8.23%, while the S&P 500 has an annualized return of 10.15% over the same period, according to data from Morningstar.

In August, ARK kept buying Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) across five funds while investors worried about an AI bubble, and it sold some Roblox shares. Check out the full story here.

Wood addressed the selloff in her latest In The Know episode on YouTube, and she thinks the market overreacted to the midterm elections. She said stocks have usually risen in the year after a midterm election, by roughly 13% to 14% in the periods she showed. She also tried to calm fears that data center projects will slow down. Wood said data centers in communities like those in Virginia have lowered property taxes and paid for new schools, and she blamed the negative headlines for hiding that. She also thinks AI spending is still at an early stage.

Wood expects AI to lift productivity, keep inflation lower than most investors expect, and push US real GDP growth to 7%. Cramer has also talked about the data center backlash. He said AI executives now face criticism over rising electricity bills, resource use and job losses, and he still likes certain AI stocks. Click to see the stocks he still likes.

Methodology

To compile this list, we reviewed ARK Investment Management's third-quarter 2026 portfolio, as disclosed in its latest 13F filing, and identified stocks that Jim Cramer has spoken positively about in his recent CNBC commentary. We prioritized well-known companies and excluded stocks in which ARK reduced its shareholdings by more than 5% during the quarter. We then ranked the 10 selected stocks in ascending order of the number of hedge funds holding stakes in them at the end of the second quarter of 2026, using Insider Monkey's database of 1,006 hedge funds. ARK's holdings and changes reflect the third quarter, while the hedge fund ownership figures reflect the second quarter. To see where ARK stood going into the year, check our list Cathie Wood 2026 Portfolio: 10 Best Stocks to Buy. For more of Cramer's recent favorites, see Jim Cramer Is Bullish on These 10 Stocks Amid Nvidia (NVDA) Controversy.
